children: By Staff Writer

India’s state-owned Engineers India Limited (EIL) has secured a contract worth more than $450 million from Nigeria’s Dangote Group to provide project management and engineering services for a planned 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery and petrochemical complex in Kenya.

The deal comes barely a week before the planned groundbreaking ceremony for the multibillion-dollar project in Lamu, marking a major step in Dangote’s expansion into East Africa’s energy sector.“Believing in EIL’s Engineering and Project Management excellence, the Dangote Group has once again joined hands with EIL… for this prestigious Kenya Project,” Aliko Dangote said in a statement cited in the company’s disclosure.
The groundbreaking ceremony is planned for September 30 at the proposed refinery site in the Lamu Special Economic Zone, and will be attended by Kenyan President William Ruto.

EIL will be the Project Management Consultant (PMC) and Engineering, Procurement and Construction Management (EPCM) consultant, giving the Indian company responsibility for coordinating key aspects of the development, including engineering, procurement, construction management, costs, schedules, quality and safety.

The contract, announced by EIL on Tuesday, is valued at more than $450 million. It covers consultancy and project-management services and should not be confused with the much larger cost of constructing the refinery, which has previously been put at between $15 billion and $17 billion.

The location of the facility gives the project access to Lamu’s deep-water port and positions the proposed refinery as part of a wider logistics and energy hub linking the Kenyan coast with landlocked markets in the region.

EIL said the new contract builds on its existing relationship with Dangote, after it provided project management and EPCM services for the Nigerian conglomerate’s 650,000-barrel-per-day refinery and petrochemical complex at Lekki.

Dangote’s Nigerian refinery has since become one of Africa’s largest refining facilities, with its current crude distillation capacity at 700,000 barrels per day. The group is also pursuing an expansion that would take the facility’s capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day.
EIL said the Kenya assignment reflected Dangote’s confidence in its ability to execute large and complex energy projects.

The Indian company, which operates under India’s Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, has extensive experience in refinery, petrochemical, gas processing and other energy infrastructure projects in Africa and the Middle East.

Its previous involvement in the Dangote refinery in Nigeria provides a direct link between the two projects, with the company having handled engineering and project-management responsibilities during development of the Nigerian facility. EIL’s earlier project documentation also records its involvement in the Dangote refinery and petrochemical complex at Lekki.
The Kenya project will be significantly larger in terms of planned crude-processing capacity than the original Nigerian refinery design and is intended to process a wider range of crude oils.

EIL said the facility is expected to strengthen fuel production in East Africa, reduce dependence on imported petroleum products, improve regional energy security and create capacity to supply refined products to international markets.
The development comes as governments seek to reduce exposure to volatile international fuel markets and improve security of petroleum supplies.

Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo depend substantially on imported refined petroleum products, making the addition of a large coastal refinery potentially significant for regional supply chains.

The proposed plant could also create a new demand centre for crude transported through the region and strengthen the strategic importance of Lamu Port, which Kenya is developing as the maritime gateway of the Lapsset corridor.
The project is also being linked to Kenya’s plans to unlock crude oil resources in Turkana.

President Ruto has said Kenya is discussing with Dangote the possibility of developing infrastructure to transport Turkana crude to Lamu for processing, although such plans remain separate from the newly announced EIL consultancy contract.

The proposed connection between Turkana’s oilfields and the Lamu refinery could, if developed, provide a domestic crude supply source for part of the facility while supporting Kenya’s ambition to move from crude exports towards greater domestic value addition.

Deputy President Kithure Kindiki on Tuesday said the refinery would help reduce Kenya’s foreign-exchange expenditure on petroleum imports while generating employment and business opportunities for communities in Lamu and the wider coastal region.“This project will reduce pressure on our foreign exchange because we spend a lot of money importing oil and number two, we are very optimistic that this project will create jobs in the region of 50,000,” Prof Kindiki said.
He added that the investment would empower communities in Lamu and the wider coast through employment and other economic opportunities.
The Deputy President also linked the refinery to Kenya’s plans to begin commercial oil production, saying the country expected its oil industry to become operational towards the end of this year.
The refinery is expected to form part of a larger industrial complex incorporating petrochemical production and supporting infrastructure.

Its proposed 700,000-barrel-per-day capacity would make it one of the largest refinery projects planned on the continent, although its eventual impact on regional fuel markets will depend on financing, construction, crude supply, infrastructure and the commercial arrangements governing product distribution.
The project also gives Dangote a significant foothold in East Africa after establishing a major refining and petrochemical base in Nigeria.

Dangote Group has operations in more than a dozen African countries and has increasingly expanded beyond its traditional cement business into energy, fertiliser and other industrial sectors. The group says its operations span 17 African countries.
Dangote is also exploring other opportunities in East Africa.

In Tanzania, the group has been discussing investments in infrastructure, energy, fertiliser and transport, while explaining its decision to locate its planned East African refinery in Lamu. Dangote has invited Tanzania to participate in the investment.
